sentences.text: The genus name Astorgosuchus merges Greek terms for merciless and crocodile, while the species name bugtiensis honors the Bugti Hills in Pakistan.
This large-bodied crocodyloid possessed a blunt snout that was short and broad, measuring only twice as long as it was wide.
Skull lengths for specific specimens are estimated at 80 to 91 centimeters, and the fifth maxillary tooth is the largest tooth in the upper jaw.
The external nostrils extend further back than in modern crocodilians, reaching the level of the fifth maxillary tooth.
The side of the lower jaw bone is heavily ornamented with deep circular holes, and the third, fourth, and fifth lower teeth are adjacent, with the fourth being the largest.
Astorgosuchus is estimated to have reached lengths of up to 7 to 8 meters.
The side of the lower jaw bone is heavily ornamented with deep circular holes.
The first crocodilian remains from the Bugti Hills were described by G. E. Pilgrim in 1908 and 1912, and the type species was originally named Crocodylus bugtiensis by Pilgrim in 1908.
The holotype specimen IM E221 consists of a left maxilla and cranial fragments found at Pishi Nala and is housed in the Indian Museum in Kolkata.

Additional remains were discovered in Baluchistan in the 1920s and presented to the Natural History Museum in London in 1925, and a maxilla fragment reported by K. N. Prasad was found on Piram Island in western India and dated to the Late Miocene.
Martin and colleagues formally created the genus Astorgosuchus in 2019.
Bite marks found on juvenile Paraceratherium bones are attributed to a large crocodile, but it is uncertain if Astorgosuchus made them.
Astorgosuchus belongs to the superfamily Crocodyloidea and is an extinct archosaurian crocodilian genus closely related to modern crocodiles.
Astorgosuchus is most closely related to the basal crocodyloid Asiatosuchus germanicus.
The involvement of the splenial in the lower jaw symphysis distinguishes Astorgosuchus from Crocodylinae and Mekosuchinae.

Astorgosuchus lived in the Bugti Hills of Balochistan, Pakistan, during the late Oligocene, and the time range for Astorgosuchus is from the Rupelian to the Chattian stages, approximately 33.9 to 23.04 million years ago.
Astorgosuchus inhabited a river and lake environment shared with rhinoceroses, chalicotheres, anthracotheres, and proboscideans.
